title: Lars Doucet, "Does Georgism Work? Five Years Later" (Center for Land Economics / Progress and Poverty Substack cross-post, 24 Sep 2026; full essay is a guest post on Astral Codex Ten)
what_was_fetched: The queue URL itself (blog.landeconomics.org) resolved to a short (~2,100-character) Substack cross-post announcement, not the essay -- it is a teaser that links out to the real piece. Fetched that teaser first (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200), confirmed it was only an announcement, then located and fetched the actual essay at https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/does-georgism-work-five-years-later (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200, 484KB HTML -> 52KB extracted text) and read it in full. Cross-checked several factual claims in the essay against the existing corpus digest by grepping for south-korea, molit, nielsson, qingdao, pittsburgh, virginia, kentucky, baden-w*, enablement -- see existing_wiki_coverage.
verdict: ENRICH research/doucet-does-georgism-work.md -- add a dated 'Five Years Later (2026)' section documenting what Doucet now retracts/revises/reaffirms from the 2021 series, per the existing page's own de-referencing-ledger convention. Light, secondary ENRICH candidates: places/south-korea.md (a new land-value-to-GDP figure, attributed to Doucet's own calculation from official MOLIT data, not an independent study) and concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md (the historical 'Somers system' of citizen-consensus land valuation, and a short account of South Korea's annual 500,000-standard-parcel national valuation cycle). NOT a NEW research page and NOT a source of new Tier-1 evidence: every specific empirical claim in the essay that the wiki lacked is either (a) Doucet's own practitioner analysis/interview-based reporting (Tier 2, per people-tiers.json), or (b) a source already fully ingested elsewhere on the wiki (see existing_wiki_coverage). research/watling-doucet-lvt-failure-exchange.md needs no new content -- the essay's Watling discussion (UK vs. Korea GDP-per-capita comparison) only reaffirms Doucet's existing rebuttal, adding one comparative statistic that is a minor, optional addition at most.
claim_grade: Tier 2 throughout (Lars Doucet, explicitly listed in sources/audit/people-tiers.json tier2). Origin/proponent claims only, never cite as settled evidence. Within that: the retrospective judgments about his own 2021 series (what aged well/poorly) are Doucet's own first-person account (C/D-claim, citable only as 'Doucet now says'); the South Korea land-value-to-GDP figures (>500% currently, 400-600% over 50+ years) are Doucet's own back-of-envelope calculation from official Korean MOLIT (Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport) data -- the underlying MOLIT data would be Tier 1 if independently verified, but as relayed here it is an unverified Tier-2 secondary calculation (D-claim pending independent check). The one specific academic citation that is new-to-Doucet's-argument -- Nielsson, Wroblewski & Yding (2024) on Danish rent control and LVT pass-through -- is NOT new to the wiki (already a full Important-tier research page).
content_summary: Structure of the essay: (I-II) recap of the 2021 series and legislative/political momentum since (Virginia/Kentucky LVT enablement laws, April 2026; Washington State bill with Sightline Institute; NY Gov. Hochul's land-value-capture authority extension for the Interborough Express; UK PM Andy Burnham; South Korea's Lee Jae-myung; Germany's Baden-Wurttemberg LVT, Jan 2025 -- ALL already on the wiki, see existing_wiki_coverage). (III) 'My theory of change was wrong' -- a strategy/movement-building reflection (overrated: online arguments; underrated: doing policymakers' homework via tools like CivicMapper and LVTShift), not an empirical claim requiring citation. (IV) Part-by-part self-assessment: Part 1 ('Is land a big deal?') 'has aged the best' -- reaffirmed, plus a new South Korea data point (land value-to-GDP >500%, historically 400-600% over 50+ years, vs. Doucet's own ~200% US estimate), sourced to MOLIT via Doucet's own interviews/analysis, not an independent citation. Part 2 (tax incidence) -- Doucet now concedes ONE narrow exception where LVT/property tax CAN pass through to tenants: under pervasive rent control plus a landlord exemption to raise rents by the tax increase, citing Nielsson, Wroblewski & Yding (2024) on Denmark -- already a full wiki research page (see existing_wiki_coverage); Doucet frames this as a narrow, mechanism-specific exception, not a general refutation, and poses four unanswered questions he says a general capitalization-denial theory would need to answer. Part 3 (assessment) -- 'aged the least well,' the most revised: (a) South Korea's national annual land-only valuation system (500,000 nationally-appraised 'standard parcels' anchoring local government valuations of all other parcels, full national cycle completed in 5 months), based on Doucet's own interviews with Korean researchers and MOLIT procedural documents -- not independently verified by the wiki; (b) Doucet now believes the traditional 'cost approach' to appraisal is 'basically fine' (a reversal from his 2021 skepticism), based on an interview with a single NC assessor (Tier 3, practitioner's own statement, not citable as a finding); (c) a historical note on the early-20th-century 'Somers system' of citizen-consensus land valuation (US, waned ~1950s), sourced to an old primary text ('The Science and Practice of Urban Land Valuation'); (d) a claim that 'a researcher recently discovered new German-language primary sources' on Qingdao/Tsingtao's colonial-era LVT -- NO researcher or publication is named, so this is NOT citable and should not be added to the wiki's tsingtao-land-tax stub without a real source. (V-VIII) Historical/biographical material (the 'closed frontier' thesis, Doucet's personal history and the founding of the Center for Land Economics) -- already substantially covered on organizations/center-for-land-economics.md and not encyclopedic content in its own right.
existing_wiki_coverage: Extremely thorough prior ingestion of the Center for Land Economics/Progress and Poverty Substack output means almost every factual thread in this essay is already on the wiki: events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md (Virginia/Kentucky/NY enablement wave), places/kentucky.md (Louisville split-rate law), places/germany.md (Baden-Wurttemberg LVT, Jan 2025), places/south-korea.md (Lee Jae-myung's land-dividend politics, Landforall.kr/Jinsu Lee, Land+Freedom Institute, the 2026 jongbusae reform -- but NOT the specific land-value-to-GDP ratio figures this essay adds), places/pittsburgh.md ('A Second Assessment Crisis, 2026' section already documents Pro-Housing Pittsburgh's OpenAVMKit-based reassessment effort in detail, matching this essay's account precisely), research/nielsson-wroblewski-yding-danish-lvt.md (full Important-tier page on the Denmark paper Doucet cites for the rent-control exception -- though the existing page's summary does not currently attribute the zero-price-effect finding to a rent-control mechanism the way Doucet's essay does; worth a T1 check against the paper itself), research/watling-doucet-lvt-failure-exchange.md (the Watling rebuttal this essay briefly reaffirms), organizations/center-for-land-economics.md (the org's founding, Miller/Doucet). No existing coverage of: the Somers system (historical assessment method), South Korea's specific land-value-to-GDP figures/MOLIT methodology, or the NC-assessor 'cost approach' interview.
uncertainties: (1) The South Korea land-value-to-GDP figures (>500%, 400-600% range) rest entirely on Doucet's own calculation from MOLIT data via his own (translated) reading of Korean-language documents -- no primary MOLIT publication or independent secondary source was located or checked; a T1 wanting to cite these numbers on-wiki should try to find and verify against an OECD or MOLIT primary figure rather than citing Doucet's number directly. (2) Doucet's claim that Nielsson et al.'s zero-price-effect result is specifically explained by Denmark's rent-control-plus-landlord-exemption mechanism was not checked against the Nielsson paper's own text in this pass -- the wiki's existing summary of that paper (research/nielsson-wroblewski-yding-danish-lvt.md) does not currently mention rent control as an explanation, so this may be Doucet's own added interpretation rather than the authors' framing; a T1 should verify before wiring it in as the paper's own finding. (3) The Qingdao 'new researcher discovery' claim is unsourced (no name, no publication) and should not be added to the wiki in that form.

title: Sacha Dray, Camille Landais & Stefanie Stantcheva, "Wealth and Property Taxation in the United States," Quarterly Journal of Economics, advance article, 4 Sep 2026 (DOI 10.1093/qje/qjag038); NBER Working Paper 31080, March 2023, revised May 2026
what_was_fetched: The OUP advance-article page was not attempted directly (flagged paywalled in the queue context). Instead located and fetched the underlying NBER working paper PDF (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w31080/w31080.pdf, curl with browser UA, HTTP 200, 8.16MB, 66 pages) -- the paper's title, abstract, JEL codes, and author list exactly match the QJE advance-article entry, and the NBER page carries a 'Revised May 2026' date consistent with a paper about to clear to a September 2026 QJE advance article. Extracted full text with PyMuPDF (2,944 lines) and read it closely: full abstract, full introduction (headline findings), the institutional-history section (Sections 2-3: the General Property Tax 1842-1933, its Depression-era demise, tax-base/tax-rate/administration features), the effective-tax-rate figures and their construction (Section 3, Figure 1 and Figure 2 notes), the Reconstruction-era Southern effective-rate discussion, and the full conclusion (Section 8). NOT read in comparable depth: the full econometric determinants-of-growth regressions (Sections 5-7 tables), the county-level data-construction appendix (Appendix III), and most appendix figures/tables beyond what the main-text figure notes describe. Also confirmed via WebSearch that alternate copies exist on SSRN (abstract_id=4407487) and Stantcheva's own Harvard site, not independently fetched since the NBER copy was authoritative and complete.
verdict: NEW research page (recommend tier Important, arguable Core given the scale/originality of the dataset and Lincoln Institute co-funding -- leave the Core/Important call to T1). This is a direct, previously-missing fill for US property-tax history, which the wiki currently covers only through scattered incidence/capitalization studies (Oates 1969, Mieszkowski, Cabral & Hoxby) with no long-run historical series. Should be wired as supports_outcomes/cross-linked to: research/saez-zucman-wealth-inequality.md (modern wealth-concentration companion -- this paper is its 19th/early-20th-century predecessor), research/oates-1969-capitalization.md, research/piketty-capital-21st-century.md, concepts/split-rate-taxation.md and any US property-tax-history material on places/pennsylvania.md or places/united-states.md. Consider whether it also warrants a place in problems/ or benefits/ given its Reconstruction/slavery findings bear on inequality-and-growth claims the wiki may already carry.
claim_grade: A-claim, Tier 1 for all three authors under EDITORIAL SS4c: Stefanie Stantcheva (Harvard/NBER/CEPR, already an established wiki-cited author via the Akcigit-Grigsby-Nicholas-Stantcheva research page), Camille Landais (LSE/CEPR), Sacha Dray (World Bank) -- all established academics with peer-reviewed public-finance/inequality bodies of work. Caveat: the fetched text is the NBER working-paper version (revised May 2026), not a copy of the actual QJE typeset advance article -- NBER working papers 'have not been peer-reviewed or been subject to review by the NBER Board' per their own disclaimer on the PDF, though the QJE advance-article listing indicates this version (or one very close to it) has now cleared QJE's peer review. A T1 should note on-wiki that the cited PDF is the NBER working-paper text, with the QJE publication as the peer-reviewed venue of record, and flag if the two are later found to differ.
content_summary: DATA: newly collected/digitized U.S. General Property Tax records (annual state reports plus decadal Census 'Wealth, Debt, and Taxation' compilations used to derive assessment ratios), yielding annual state-level wealth series 1850 (or earlier)-1935, decadal county-level series 1850-1930, and a national series from the early 1800s-1935 -- the authors describe this as the first comparably comprehensive, high-frequency, long-run sub-national U.S. property/wealth dataset. HEADLINE PROPERTY-TAX FINDINGS (the queue's specific ask): total property tax revenue as a share of GDP was below 2% in 1850, more than doubled to about 5% of GDP by the 1920s (the eve of the Great Depression), then fell sharply to roughly 2.5-3% of GDP in the 1950s and after, where it has stayed (Figure 1). Total property tax revenue as a share of TOTAL government revenue fell from 38.8% (1927) to 25.2% (1938) to 8.1% (1946) (citing Benson et al. 1965) -- the paper attributes the post-Depression decline to three interacting causes: federal-government expansion (New Deal/Social Security), new state revenue sources (income/sales/motor-fuel taxes), and Depression-era plus postwar exemptions (homestead exemptions, rate limits). EFFECTIVE RATES: municipal/lower-jurisdiction effective rates rose from about 0.3% (1850) to about 1% (1930); combined county+state rates stayed roughly flat around 0.3%; total effective property tax rate rose from about 0.6% (1850) to about 1.35% (1930); in 1920 specifically, the average total effective rate was 1.4% (average city rate 1%, county 0.24%, state 0.16%), with wide geographic variation (roughly 0.5% to over 3% across jurisdictions) (Figure 2). WEALTH-SERIES FINDINGS: rapid national wealth growth after the Civil War, outpacing income growth; persistent, non-converging spatial inequality across counties/states through at least 1930 (no 'sigma-convergence'; top-10%-of-counties wealth share rose; slow 'beta-convergence' versus what income data alone would suggest, driven mainly by the South). SLAVERY/RECONSTRUCTION: in Georgia, Florida and Alabama, enslaved people accounted for over 50% of recorded property value before the Civil War; excluding enslaved property, true Southern wealth fell by more than 25% between 1860 and 1870, and Southern effective property tax rates rose sharply during Reconstruction as new, previously-disenfranchised political coalitions pushed for higher rates. County-level growth determinants (1870-1930, 60-year horizon): climate/topography/soil productivity and coastal proximity predict initial wealth; literacy (human capital) predicts both initial wealth and subsequent growth; 1870 population (agglomeration) predicts faster subsequent growth; higher initial top-10% wealth concentration is robustly NEGATIVELY correlated with 60-year subsequent county wealth growth, controlling for a wide set of geographic/demographic/economic factors, and this operates partly through slower subsequent literacy gains in more-unequal counties. LAND vs. OTHER PROPERTY (the queue's other specific ask): the paper does NOT isolate pure land value from buildings/improvements anywhere in the sections read -- its wealth decomposition is 'real property' (land+buildings combined) vs. 'personal property' vs. (for Southern states specifically) 'enslaved property.' The conclusion explicitly flags 'a finer analysis of different types of wealth' as future work, not something this paper delivers. This is an important caveat for Georgist use: it is a wealth-and-property-tax-history paper, not a land-value-specific study.
existing_wiki_coverage: No existing wiki page on U.S. property-tax history at this scale or period; the digest's ~20 property-tax research pages are mostly modern incidence/capitalization/behavioral studies (Cabral & Hoxby 2012 on salience; Mieszkowski on the 'new view'; Oates 1969 on capitalization; Coven on lock-in) or single-place case studies (Pittsburgh, various African/Latin American/Asian country studies), none reaching before the mid-20th century except brief historical asides on individual pages (e.g., places/pittsburgh.md's 1913 Graded Tax Law). research/saez-zucman-wealth-inequality.md is the closest existing companion (modern, 1913-2012, capitalized-income method) -- this paper is effectively its 19th/early-20th-century predecessor using a completely different data source (direct assessment records rather than capitalized income flows), and the two should cross-link. research/piketty-capital-21st-century.md (wealth-income ratios) is another natural cross-link. No existing coverage anywhere of the General Property Tax as an institution, its Depression-era demise, or long-run US effective property tax rates.
uncertainties: (1) Did not read the full econometric growth-determinants tables (Sections 5-7) or the data-construction appendix (Appendix III) in comparable depth to the main narrative sections -- a T1 drafting precise regression coefficients or robustness-check details should read those sections directly. (2) Did not verify whether the QJE-published advance-article text is identical to the NBER working paper (revised May 2026) used here -- flagged above; recommend citing the NBER PDF explicitly as the source consulted, with a note that QJE is the peer-reviewed venue of record, and revisiting once QJE assigns final volume/issue/pages. (3) Only skimmed the appendix figure notes (e.g., Appendix Figure A12 on Connecticut property composition, A26/A27 on exemption ratios) rather than reading the appendix tables themselves -- there may be additional land/real-estate-specific detail buried there that a closer read would surface. (4) Did not check whether 'land' is ever isolated as a sub-category of 'real property' anywhere in the 66 pages beyond the conclusion's explicit statement that this is left to future work -- treated that statement as authoritative but a full-text keyword pass beyond the grep performed here was not exhaustive.

title: Kartika Listriana & Walter Timo de Vries, "Cultural Heritage, Land Value Dynamics, and Land Value Capture Governance in Asia: A Systematic Literature Review," International Journal of Sustainable Development and Planning 21(8):3423-3437, IIETA, 31 Aug 2026 (DOI 10.18280/ijsdp.210802)
what_was_fetched: Fetched the IIETA landing page directly (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200), located the direct PDF download link embedded in the page (iieta.org/download/file/fid/199431), and fetched the PDF itself (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200, 1.2MB, 15 pages) -- no paywall or access barrier encountered; open access as the queue context indicated. Extracted full text with PyMuPDF and read the entire paper: abstract, introduction, literature review/conceptual framework, full methodology section (search strategy, PRISMA screening, and a notable revision-stage 'corrective audit'), full results/discussion (corpus profile, heritage-value-creation findings, governance-conditions typology with two summary tables), and the full conclusions/limitations section.
verdict: ENRICH concepts/land-value-capture.md -- add a dated subsection ('Heritage-Led LVC in Asia (2026)') under the page's existing 'Recent Case Studies and Critiques (2025-26)' pattern, which already handles dated additions with explicit sourcing caveats (see Grand Paris Express, CaCHE/England, San Antonio TIRZ entries there). NOT a dedicated research page and NOT Core/Important tier, for three concrete reasons the venue-honesty instruction asked to weigh: (a) IIETA/IJSDP is a broad-scope, lower-tier open-access publisher, not a specialist planning or public-finance journal; (b) the review's own methodology section discloses real limitations candidly -- single-reviewer screening (no dual-reviewer check, explicit 'residual risk of selection bias' the authors themselves flag), and a confusing revision-stage 'corrective audit' in which the original 2025 record-level search export was not preserved and the final N=20 analytical corpus had to be reconstructed de novo from a 64-reference working pool after peer review flagged missing studies -- the paper is honest about this but it is a real quality flag; (c) the review explicitly declines quantitative synthesis ('does not justify statistical pooling or meta-analysis') and reports no pooled or quantified effect sizes of its own -- it is a qualitative governance-conditions typology, useful as a navigational/framing source but not as evidence of a magnitude. If cited, tier should be Supplementary with the venue and methodology caveats stated in the Sources annotation, matching the queue's own suggested likely verdict.
claim_grade: C-claim navigational/framing source. Author tier: Walter Timo de Vries (TU Munich, Chair of Land Management) is plausibly Tier 1 by the SS4c rubric (established academic with a peer-reviewed land-administration research record) but is not on the confirmed tier1 list in people-tiers.json -- a T1 should judge independently if citing him by name. Kartika Listriana's academic standing is unconfirmed (the corresponding-author email format, go24bir@mytum.de, is consistent with a TU Munich graduate-student ID rather than a faculty account); treat as unconfirmed tier, do not present as an established-scholar voice. The venue itself (IJSDP/IIETA) should not be cited the way a top field journal would be -- attribute claims as 'a 2026 systematic review found...' rather than 'research shows...'.
content_summary: SAMPLE: a reconstructed analytical corpus of 20 studies (2018-2025, concentrated in 2020 and 2023), drawn from an initial 1,047-record search across Scopus/Web of Science/ScienceDirect/SpringerLink/Google Scholar (Apr-May 2025), following PRISMA 2020 screening down through 799 (post-dedup) -> 524 (post title-check) -> 90 (full-text assessed) -> 20 retained, THEN a separate revision-stage re-screening of a 64-reference working pool that reconstructed the same N=20 total via a different process after peer review (see verdict/uncertainties -- this two-stage history is disclosed by the authors themselves in the methodology and conclusion). CITIES/COUNTRIES: China, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, plus one comparative China/US study. Named direct 'intersection' case studies (heritage + LVC together): Wu et al. on heritage-protection value capture at West Lake (China); Zhao et al. on heritage-led development, real-estate valorisation and 'uneven community outcomes' in Xi'an (China); two Indonesian studies modelling heritage ecosystems, land value and LVC-based financing at Kota Lama Tangerang; a Dihua Street (Taiwan) case where transfer of development rights is found to support historic-district preservation 'while moderating displacement and rent pressure.' Non-intersection but cited property-market evidence: Singapore conservation designation is 'associated with positive but spatially heterogeneous residential price effects and unequal premiums across property segments' (no percentage given in the review's own text); Hong Kong's Wan Chai revitalization is 'associated with value enhancement in nearby retail properties' (again no quantified magnitude given). TYPOLOGY: the review organizes LVC instruments (betterment levies, development charges, land value taxation, land readjustment, TDR, negotiated developer obligations, joint development, public-land strategies, tax/revenue-based mechanisms) and identifies seven recurring governance conditions for heritage-related LVC feasibility: legal/regulatory clarity, fiscal capacity and revenue management, LVC instrument design/fit, financing markets and PPP business models, zoning/TOD/FAR and spatial-planning integration, valuation and cadastral (data) capacity, and stakeholder legitimacy/equity safeguards -- presented in two summary tables. The review also proposes a four-phase periodization of the LVC-in-Asia literature (2016-18 emerging; 2019-21 growth/feasibility; 2022-23 'mature'/operational, betterment levies and TOD; 2024-25 'sunset', PPP-LVC convergence and FAR tools) and a VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence bibliometric map, explicitly used only as a 'descriptive... not... causal' diagnostic. QUANTIFIED FINDINGS: none -- the review states directly that its N=20 corpus 'is too small to support robust network inference' and that its findings 'should be read as a synthesis of evidence-supported relationships... not as a validated causal model'; it explicitly states current studies do NOT establish that captured LVC revenues have 'systematically produced conservation, resilience, or equity outcomes across Asian cities.'
existing_wiki_coverage: No existing coverage anywhere in the corpus digest of heritage-linked land value capture, West Lake, Xi'an, Kota Lama Tangerang, or Dihua Street; the only 'heritage' hit in the digest is the unrelated concepts/common-heritage-of-mankind.md (seabed/resource-rents). concepts/land-value-capture.md is the natural and only strong target -- its existing 'Recent Case Studies and Critiques (2025-26)' section already follows exactly the pattern this source would fit (dated sub-bullet, explicit sourcing/access caveats, e.g. the Grand Paris Express entry's 'no claim below the abstract level is made' framing). No existing page on Singapore's conservation program, Hong Kong's Wan Chai, or Taiwan's Dihua Street TDR case specifically (Taiwan is otherwise covered via concepts/land-value-increment-tax.md and research/chu-taiwan-property-tax-incidence.md, unrelated to heritage).
uncertainties: (1) None of the 20 underlying primary studies (Wu et al., Zhao et al., the Tangerang studies, the Dihua Street study, the Singapore/Hong Kong property-market studies) were independently fetched or verified -- everything reported here is filtered through this review's own synthesis and paraphrase; a T1 wanting to cite a specific finding (e.g., the Singapore price-premium result) should locate and read the underlying primary study rather than relying on the review's characterization. (2) The review's own methodology contains an internally-disclosed inconsistency worth a T1's attention before citing its 'N=20' figure as a clean, simple count: the documented primary PRISMA sequence (1,047->799->524->90->20) is presented as internally consistent, but a separate revision-stage 'corrective audit' of a 64-reference working pool reconstructed the same N=20 total through a different process (15 references meeting criteria from the 64, plus 5 more from a targeted sensitivity search) after peer review flagged omitted intersection studies -- the authors state 'a one-to-one statement of which original study was replaced... cannot be made reliably' because the original record-level export was not preserved. This is disclosed by the authors themselves (not something I am inferring), but it is exactly the kind of venue/rigor issue EDITORIAL asked to be judged honestly rather than glossed over. (3) Walter Timo de Vries's tier status is my own rubric judgment, not a name already on people-tiers.json's confirmed list -- flag for T1 to formally decide.

(4) WebFetch tool directly on the same PDF URL -> HTTP 403 (same Cloudflare wall via a different fetch path). (5) WebFetch DID succeed on the IAAO abstract/landing page (researchexchange.iaao.org/jptaa/vol10/iss2/1/, no Cloudflare wall on that specific page) and returned the verified abstract, full citation (vol/issue/pages), and confirmation of the World Bank conference origin. (8) Checked Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar APIs by DOI -> both confirm 'closed access', no open-access location recorded anywhere. FULL-TEXT TARGET PAPER WAS NOT OBTAINED. As a substitute, located and fully fetched a different, closely related work by the same author from the same period: Lawrence C. Walters, 'Are Property-Related Taxes Effective Value Capture Instruments?' (ch. 8, pp. 187-205, in Gregory K. Ingram & Yu-Hung Hong, eds., Value Capture and Land Policies, Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, 2012) -- direct PDF link found via WebSearch (lincolninst.edu/app/uploads/legacy-files/pubfiles/2181_1506_LP2011_ch08...pdf), fetched with curl/browser UA (HTTP 200, 682KB, 34 pages -- includes surrounding book front matter), extracted with PyMuPDF, and read in full.
verdict: NEW research page is defensible on Walters's citation standing and Tier-1 status by the SS4c rubric, but should be flagged to T1 as built from INCOMPLETE access to the actual target paper. Recommend T1 make one more attempt to obtain the real JPTAA 2013 full text (institutional journal access, interlibrary loan, or a direct request to Walters at BYU) before publishing; failing that, a NEW page can still be built responsibly right now IF it clearly separates two distinct works in its Sources section: (a) the JPTAA 2013 paper, citable only via its verified abstract plus the queue's own framing (cost-recovery vs. unearned-increment rationales analyzed across country cases) -- marked explicitly as abstract-only; and (b) the fully-read 2012 Lincoln Institute book chapter, a DIFFERENT, U.S.-specific empirical paper by the same author from the same period, used for the instrument taxonomy, the four practical conditions, the Denmark/Paris country examples, and its own distinct empirical contribution (a novel national cash-flow-based property-value metric applied to 156 US metro areas). Do NOT present the chapter's content as though it were the JPTAA paper's content -- they are related but not identical works, and the chapter contains no explicit 'cost-recovery vs. unearned-increment' framing by that name, nor any of the queue's expected cross-country examples beyond Denmark and 19th-century Paris.
claim_grade: A/B-claim, Tier 1 by the SS4c rubric (an established academic -- Lawrence C. Walters, Brigham Young University -- with a peer-reviewed and World Bank/Lincoln Institute-level publication record on land value capture; 54+ citations per the queue's own framing). Walters is NOT currently on sources/audit/people-tiers.json's tier1_confirmed list -- recommend T1 add him there if this page proceeds. The JPTAA abstract itself is A-claim (peer-reviewed journal, DOI-confirmed via Crossref: is_oa=false, closed access, published 1 June 2013). The Lincoln Institute chapter is also A-claim (peer-reviewed-adjacent, edited academic volume, Lincoln Institute of Land Policy).
content_summary: FROM THE VERIFIED JPTAA ABSTRACT (target paper, abstract-only access): the paper 'examines how governments implement land value capture (LVC)... The author analyzes country-specific cases to determine which policy objectives are pursued and assesses the practical feasibility of LVC strategies' -- i.e., a cross-national comparative review of WHY countries pursue LVC (cost recovery for specific infrastructure vs. capturing the broader 'unearned increment') and HOW FEASIBLE the available instruments are in practice. No country names or specific instrument findings are given in the abstract itself. FROM THE FULLY-READ 2012 LINCOLN INSTITUTE CHAPTER (a distinct, U.S.-focused companion work, NOT the JPTAA paper): opens with the same UN-HABITAT 'unearned increment' framing (Vancouver Action Plan, UN 1976) and states four necessary conditions for property-tax-based LVC to work in practice: (1) public investment/growth must raise private land values; (2) the increase must be identified by the assessment process and incorporated into taxable value; (3) the taxing jurisdiction must maintain an effective rate sufficient to raise the resulting tax bill; (4) the resulting revenue increase must be adequate to cover the required share of infrastructure cost. INSTRUMENT TAXONOMY (Table 8.1 in the chapter): one-time fees/taxes -- development/impact fees (cost-recovery-oriented: 'the fees assessed should approximate the actual costs incurred', found only modestly effective per the literature reviewed), estate tax (very limited LVC relevance in the US system), capital gains tax (uncertain, mostly a state/federal rather than local instrument), transfer tax (disconnected from LVC since it taxes full value, not the increment), betterment tax (explicitly increment-based -- 'an explicit attempt to share in a private value gain resulting from a public action', requires sustained political will); and the ANNUAL property tax, which the chapter argues can be the most stable LVC mechanism IF values are updated regularly and rates capture the increase. Nontax LVC tools discussed: developer land sale (Denmark's Orestad district, City of Copenhagen + national government partnership, financed by gross-floor-space sales to developers plus property tax and borrowing, ~EUR175 million project) and project-related land sale (19th-century Haussmann redesign of Paris, financed via land sales following legally-enabled expropriations); also tax increment financing (TIF), reviewing a genuinely mixed empirical literature (Man & Rosentraub 1998; Carroll 2008; Dye & Merriman 2000; Youngman 2011 -- 'a plethora of economic studies have reached no consensus as to the effect of TIF on economic growth'). The chapter's OWN distinct empirical contribution: a new method for estimating aggregate property value from NIPA (national accounts) free-cash-flow data, applied to a panel of 156 US metropolitan statistical areas (1994-2006) -- finds a 1% increase in the cash-flow-based value metric produces a statistically significant 0.27% increase in property tax revenue 3-5 years later (fixed-effects model, R^2=0.58), and that transportation capital outlays are recouped via increased property tax revenue within about one year while utility outlays take up to ~20 years -- concluding that 'despite the potential challenges created by property tax limitation efforts, annual property taxes appear to be effective at capturing increased real estate values' in the U.S., though state-level assessment/levy/revenue limitation laws pose a real risk to this (only 4 US states have no such limits).
